prize_parts.citation: For a body of work that remakes the borders between lyric, essay, narrative and the book as object, in a sustained dialogue with antiquity in which formal invention carries grief, desire and the limits of language.

statement.case_for: After the round-1 exchange my first choice is still Anne Carson, but the basis for it is narrower. Her voice is highly recognizable. In Autobiography of Red the Geryon material becomes a verse novel about desire and estrangement. In Nox elegy becomes an archival, physical object organized around the death of a brother. In both, the formal invention serves the emotional and intellectual substance and does not stand in for it. Scholarship, translation and poetry read as one practice over several decades, so the achievement is not a single-book reputation. The exchange led me to tighten the citation. It should rest on the original writing, meaning the verse novel, the elegy and the essay-poems. Translation and classical scholarship are the ground the writing grows from, and I no longer name translation as a separate claim. A citation resting on the novelty of hybridity would not be sufficient, and the wording above is meant to avoid that. The configuration is unchanged. The citation is tightened. This rests on public knowledge of the works. I have not independently verified or re-read any text for this stage.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that Carson's most radical books depend on typography, physical design and classical context, so they cannot be fully judged in translation. The corpus is mostly short and fragmentary in shape, and the argument from sustained breadth is harder to make than for a large architectural oeuvre. Sem-Sandberg's doubt about consistency across the experimental and performance-oriented projects is a fair one, and I cannot fully answer it. I have not verified that the later work matches the best-known books. If the committee's standard for whole-oeuvre significance is mainly cumulative large-scale architecture, Cărtărescu fits that standard better, and I would then have to ask whether my preference rests on a standard the will actually requires.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a recognizable, densely patterned voice and an architecture of memory, body and dream that extends across volumes. She ranks Carson fifth, asks whether Carson reads as lasting literature or as a learned game, and doubts that a short hybrid corpus has the breadth of a large-scale oeuvre. She also agrees with my caution that a citation must not rest on hybridity alone.
responses.response: Mattson's own round-1 reply left the case for Carson open, saying it is substantial and her ranking may understate it. I take that seriously. The test she applies to any case built on formal novelty is the right one, and I would apply it to Carson first. My answer is the same as before. In Nox and Autobiography of Red the apparatus is how the grief and longing are reached, so I do not read it as a game. I still concede that breadth is where Cărtărescu is the more natural fit. On Cărtărescu, I accept her conclusion that depth is the stronger reading of the density. But she also says she cannot support that from close reading here, and I cannot either. A reading of the later volumes by someone who knows the Romanian could change my order. I do not want to treat the architecture of his project as settled evidence of depth before that.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson third. He accepts that a developing oeuvre is the strongest answer to his doubt about Carson's consistency. He would anchor a Cărtărescu citation in the prose project, with poetry as foundation rather than a co-equal claim. He also asks whether the late novels' intensity is sustained or merely maintained.
responses.response: I accept his framing of the open question: whether the late volumes deepen the architecture or re-run its obsessions. It is a question about the texts, and I cannot answer it from the supplied evidence. On the chair's question whether poetry should be named in a B029 citation, I agree with him that it should appear only as the base of the prose project, because translation coverage of the poetry is thin and I would not claim an independent judgment of it. On Carson, his doubt is about the margins and not about the best books. I think a citation resting on the core avoids it. I also grant that he has the better argument on scale. Scale and depth are different measures, though, and I do not think the will limits the standard to the first of them.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first, for a remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and argument with the inherited tradition. He accepts that durability should be tested on the poems and not on historical influence. He says he cannot show the later collections sustain the early level, and he would want specialist reports on Arabic poetry to address this. He also asks what would lead members who ranked him low to reassess.
responses.response: I accept that the test is the poems and not the history, and he states it honestly. I ranked Adonis seventh because of the limits of my own reading. I do not doubt the importance of his work. A specialist report that separates the continuing force of the later collections from the influence of the early ones would be the kind of evidence that could make me reassess. I cannot say now that it would move him ahead of my first two choices, and I will not promise a move I cannot justify. His point that Carson's design-dependent works are not judged from a secure position either is fair. I would say only that for Carson the uncertainty is about format, while for Adonis it is about prosody and sound, and the committee cannot close either gap by assertion. I also agree with him that the fact that a body of work translates more easily should not by itself decide between candidates.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Tawada first and Cărtărescu second, and Carson third. She argues that formal variety across genres and two writing languages should weigh above architectural scale. She asks whether Carson's aggregate has the breadth of reach the will's framing may favor. She says a Carson citation should rest on original work and not on translation and scholarship.
responses.response: Swärd and I agree on the point that a Carson citation should rest on original work, and I have adjusted my wording to reflect it. Her argument for Tawada is the strongest form of the case that formal method distributed across genres should count as sustained achievement, and I take it as seriously as I do the argument from scale. It is why B001 remains among my alternatives. I find it hard to separate Carson from Tawada by saying that one has the broader reach. Both make the formal argument, and both depend on translation coverage that I cannot measure. My reading of the will's 'idealistic direction' is the same as before. I do not think it requires social or historical reach in subject matter. I do not rank Tawada above Carson, but that is a judgment of closeness. The evidence available to me does not decide it. Neither of us can say whether Tawada's formal method holds in the later novels, and she has said as much herself.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She would rest the citation on the encounter between ancient and modern writing and its formal invention, and not on hybridity as such. She accepts that her own knowledge of Cărtărescu's poetry is thinner than her knowledge of his novels.
responses.response: Carlberg's citation wording centres the ancient-modern encounter and leaves translation out of the claim, and I have moved toward it in my revised wording. We differ only slightly. I still want the book as object to be named, since Nox cannot be described without it, but I accept that this is the part least verifiable in translation. We both reach the same limit on Cărtărescu's poetry. The chair asked whether the shared translation uncertainty is being used to separate candidates it does not separate. For my part, I do not use it to rank Carson above Cărtărescu. It affects both, in different ways.

uncertainties: How much of Carson's achievement survives in translation, especially the works that depend on typography, physical design and classical context, remains unresolved.
I have not verified that her later work sustains the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox, and the consistency of her many experimental projects is something I cannot settle.

Whether whole-oeuvre significance should be judged by cumulative architecture (Cărtărescu) or by formal renewal across genres (Carson, Tawada) is a judgment about the will that I cannot settle from the evidence supplied.

If B012 does not reach a majority, I could support B029 as a laureate on the stated criteria, and I would put B001 after it. I state this as a literary reading and not as a way to seek consensus. Whether Cărtărescu's later novels deepen or repeat the earlier architecture is the open question that would most affect my order.
My ability to assess Adonis's Arabic prosody and Tawada's Japanese and German texts is limited by translation coverage, so my ranking of them is provisional.
My judgments rest on public knowledge and the longlist summaries. I have not independently verified or re-read any text.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no connection to any shortlisted writer. My own practice draws on myth, ekphrasis and women's artistic lives, which touches themes in some candidates' work. I treat that as context and not as evidence of a preference or a reason for recusal. The profile records that I was a co-opted member in 2024 and a full member in the 2025 and 2026 listings. I have not verified that independently.
